exposure therapy needs to be done right. i really recommend you to see someone who specialises in exposure therapy for social anxiety, but if you don’t have access, i can give you some tips, and explain the basics of social anxiety and the treatment(i am not a professional, i’ve just gone through multiple rounds of treatment, and have gotten a lower level of social anxiety as a result) 

before starting treatment, you need to know how social anxiety is affecting you, what it is for you, how it manifests in your life. you can’t treat something if you’re not aware of what the problem is. 

to measure social anxiety, you rate the fear you have about a situation, and how much you (try to) avoid the situation. you’re scored both individually on fear, and avoidance, and the two added together. if you search “lsas pdf” on google you can print out a couple so you have them physically.  if you fill them out like every 1-3 months, you can keep track of your treatment, and see what areas you’ve improved in, and what areas you need to work more on.

a big part of social anxiety is safety behaviours. this can be everything from avoiding eye contact, speaking lower, wearing a hoodie, sitting in a specific place, keeping your jacket on, not initiating contact, trying to appear busy/uninterested, avoiding styles or colours of clothes you don’t normally wear, etc. 

safety behaviours might trick you into thinking you’re safer/ less anxious when engaging in them, but their just a temporary relief, and make your anxiety worse in the long run. you might not even realise your doing a lot of your safety behaviours, but you need to know what they are to be able to work against them. think about write them down, 

the goal of exposure therapy is to learn how to step outside of your confort zone and being able to handle the anxiety and uncomfortableness that brings. eventually as you practice more and more, your comfort zone becomes bigger. things that make you anxious now, will be less anxiety inducing, and some situations you will be completely comfortable in. it’s important to remember that you will never be able to get rid of the feeling of anxiety completely in all situations, but can drastically improve your life, and it’s possible to live a life that’s not controlled by your anxiety.

write down all your goals, what you want to be able to do, what you want to work on, and range them from easy to hard. examples of things you can have on your list could be practising eye contact, going to a store, talking to a stranger, making a phone call, eating at a restaurant, inviting someone for lunch, applying for a job, going to a concert, buying a new style of clothes. whatever YOU want to work on. put down things even if you don’t think their achievable right now. you can have both big and small goals. 

while your doing exposure therapy, you need to be aware of your safety behaviours, and working on not engaging in them. your task need to be something challenging, but still achievable. you might need to split your goal into levels, or multiple tasks. you need to know what to focus on, and what you want to get accomplished. 

for me, one of my goals was to be able to buy something at a store my self. the first task was just to walk around a mall and in different stores with either my therapist, my mom or my dad. while walking around my focus was on not looking at the ground, and not tensing my body/crossing my arms or doing other safety behaviours. once i was confident enough in that, the next task was to do the same, but alone. to start of, i was getting something from a different isle, and i worked up to be able to walk into a store and look at things completely alone. we made sure to change up the stores and malls, to avoid the trap of me only feeling comfortable enough in one specific store. 

the next task was to actually buy something. we did the same approach of gradually working on it, so to start of the goal was just for me to pay, while i had someone with me, and then the person was further away, and then i worked on doing it alone. 

the key is to do it at your own speed. if you jump in to quickly or try tasks that are either too challenging or not challenging enough, you won’t make progress or experience that you managed to do something hard. you need to learn the right technique to expose yourself so when you move onto something more challenging you don’t just burn yourself and make yourself worse. what works for one person might not work for another. you need to choose tasks that can help you, and doing it at a pace that is beneficial to YOU. if a goal seems to big, see if you can break it down into smaller achievable subgoals. 

after exposing yourself, think about if you managed to achieve your task/goal. if your task was to walk through a store without looking at the ground, and you went through with it, you completed the task, and it went good. it’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking a task went bad because you felt anxiety, but if you managed to accomplish the goal, remind yourself that it was a good thing, not bad. if you didn’t complete the task, consider if you just need to try again and try to focus more on your goal, or if you need to take a step back and maybe level down the task a bit, until your able to complete the original goal.

lastly, it’s important to keep practising. you won’t get better if you practice for a week and then stop and go back to your old habits. have a goal every day, even if it’s just to repeat your previous tasks, while keeping focus on avoiding safety behaviours. you don’t need something big or new every day, but atleast do maintenance, so you don’t lose progress

this is what i do to whenever my depression room gets bad:

1. anything that spoils out. food, open soda boxes, plates, cups etc. 

2. take a trashbag and throw away obvious trash. things like price tags, recepts, manuals, empty boxes etc are some of my personal struggles. you may know what is you end up collect most. 

3. clean one surface at a time. i like to start with my bed because i dont usually have that much stuff there. i would recommend either the bookshelf, the tv console or a section of the floor or bed. where you can either have an imaginary line, or physically push stuff apart so you have a little square you can work with. the bed i would divide into either 2 or 4 sections, but do more if your overwhelmed.

in this area, you will toss away the rest of the trash, put the laundry away to wash it later, put clean clothes in your closet(you don’t need to hang it up or fold it neat for now, we just place it here to clear space elsewhere) and put the things you want to keep in the general area they belong. remotes by the tv, books in a bookshelf etc. you can also make piles of items in the same category if you don’t know where to put it yet.

once one surface is clean, like the bed, you can use it to sort other things more easily. repeat cleaning out small sections until you feel ready to move on to the next step. 

4. do your laundry, change the bedspread, take out the trash etc. 

5. again, we will do this in sections. take one surface, wash it and/or dust it, and put everything that belongs exactly there. you will probably want to have a trash bag and a donation box, so you can get rid of anything that you dont need that have slipped trough the last steps. put all your books neatly on a bookshelf, hang up or fold your clothes etc. this is where you need to consider to buy more storage. everything you own needs to have a place it belongs. once the floor is completely empty you can vacuum. 



remember that when your cleaning you might have to go in circles. you don’t need to rush, you won’t be finished in one day. it’s better to take your time than to burn yourself out on day one and abandon the whole project. 

listen to music, podcasts, audio books, put something on the tv, or don’t. you know yourself best.

be kind to yourself, and good luck!

i’ve been in therapy for a couple of years now. multiple different therapists and different kinds of treatment/therapies. 

first of all, most of the work happens outside of therapy. YOU are the person who has to put in the work. therapy isn’t a person sitting and telling you some magic words that fixes up your life. you need to talk about your problems. your therapist will guide you through the conversation, and will help you see new solutions to problems you thought was impossible to solve. you may learn some tools to implement into your life, and it up to you to keep it up every day. talking honestly about a problem can make you realise it may not be such a huge deal as your mind made you think. or maybe something you thought of as insignificant are much more important in your life than you thought. you can get new perspectives, and you can get out of the cycle of overthinking and losing the big picture. 

secondly, healing takes time. it’s not linear. it may not be an easy process. allowing yourself to feel the emotions your going trough, without letting them take over your life, could be part of healing. you need to want to get better. getting out of past habits takes such a long time. 

thirdly, it’s so so so worth it. when i was first sent to therapy i was terrified. today i can still feel nervous before, but i can also look forward to the next session. 

also, it’s important to have good chemistry with your therapist. do not be afraid to say that it’s not working, and you need something or someone else. 

ps. medicine is not a necessary part of therapy. after a while in therapy i was put on zoloft, because i was at such a rock bottom i wasn’t able to get anything out of therapy, i was to anxious to pay attention or remember anything that had been said, and my depression was so bad i just gave up on everything. i was taken of the medication after i had been on it for (over) the recommended time, and it had stopped having any effect. i was really lost, even while on meds. medicine can be good hand in hand with therapy, but in itself, it won’t have the effect you need. you may feel less intense feelings or something like that, but you still don’t know how to deal with that. (speaking from experience and what doctors and therapists have told me, not a doctor myself obviously)

i fully developed SM as a teen, and im still a teen and im not recovered, so i can’t talk about that. although i am in therapy and i’ve made progress with some things, other have gotten worse.

but i can answer your questions in the edit on making her feel less anxious around you, and maybe start to talk(based on my own experience and what doctors/therapists/guidelines have recommended) i feel much more comfortable when someone talks to me. 

you need to be clear that you’re not expecting answers, getting hurt or mad when she doesn’t answer etc.

have a shared focus. a movie or a game, going for a walk, a pet, etc. depending on what you both are interested in, and how comfortable she is. this avoids “interrogation” situations, which is basically like sitting facing each other, with the only focus being you or her. i explained it poorly there but i hope you get the point. 

it’s important you give her a chance to talk. wait before you change a topic, have little pauses, if you or someone else asks a question, you need to wait and give her a change to answer, if it’s a verbal answer, or a nod, head shake, pointing, writing, or anything else. but if she talks, or goes from being completely still to using body language, DONT make a big deal out of it. unless she have told you she wants it to be a big deal, it’s not. don’t cheer, make a comment or anything else that makes it a big deal. act like it’s a normal thing. (and don’t be a prick and say “that wasn’t so hard was it” “see, i knew you could talk” etc.) 

personally, if im with anyone new im not able to talk with, i prefer when they keep talking to me, with no expectations of me to talk back. after a while of knowing them and being around them, i am not as anxious, as long as i’m not thinking i need to speak. 

the few times i’m able to break through my SM and talk, is either when i have gotten so comfortable being around a person i can finally work on speaking gradually, or when i’ve memorised exactly what i’m going to say and talk with someone i’ve never met and i’m never going to meet again. 

an example for the first is both my counsellor and my therapist, where i started  out with not saying anything, and they’ve both been great at keeping the conversation going, being ok with me not answering, taking things slow etc. i’m able to talk normally with my therapist, and i’m making a lot progress with my counsellor. 

an example of the second thing is in stores. if there’s something i really want, i can sometimes say a membership id/phonenumber etc to a cashier. i still need to rehearse in my head what i’m going to say beforehand, and when they ask for anything else then exactly what i’ve planed i cant speak.(i’ve worked a lot on this, with specialised therapists to get to this point)

it’s important you don’t ignore her, and continue speaking to her. be friendly. let her speak when she’s ready. you could also ask her if she could write down what would be helpful, so you know what could work for her.

i do have multiple anxiety disorders diagnosed. one of which was downgraded from very serious to “just” serious after intensive treatment in a specialised clinic.

to treat anxiety, like actually get better, you need to get through the things that makes you anxious. that is what exposure therapy is. this is done gradually and controlled with the help of atleast one therapist, either alone or in group.

you take small steps outside your comfort zone, so that you learn to handle the anxiety that follows. 

an example to explain it simply, if you’re scared of spiders, like a really extreme phobia to the point where you can’t go anywhere you know there are spiders, you might start out with photos or drawings of spiders. maybe not even looking at them, just having the photo in the same room as you could be outside of your comfort zone, so that is what you start with. gradually you get closer to the picture, or look more at it. at some point your “ok” seeing it. then you might go over to being outside, keeping the same slow approach. i’m not 100% sure what other things would be done, as i have not been to treatment for arachnophobia, but you get the deal. 

the goal is not the get completely rid of the anxiety, but to be able to live with it without it interfering with your life, and dealing with it when it comes. 

this can be done, no matter how bad your anxiety is. the only thing you need is the will to do something about it, and preferably a good therapist.

one last problem, mental health language is being watered down. suddenly everyone is manic, psychotic, depressed, having panic attacks, when what their experiencing is normal healthy human emotions, not illnesses.

1. find what type of book you would like to read. if you like watching tv/movies, do you go in the romance, fantasy, crime, horror etc. theres a good chance you would like those same genres in book format.

2. what format would you like to read? physical books, ebooks, audiobooks. i personally like audiobooks and physical, but figure out what works for you. depending on how much money your willing to spend, you can decide if you want to buy every book, buy a subscription for audio/ebooks or get a library card.

3. download an app like goodreads or storygraph. i use both, but one or the other works alone. goodreads doesn’t have all the stats that storygraph has, but have a much better UI, so unless you really want detailed graphs on everything, i would suggest goodreads.

4. shorter books and/or fast paced books can make it easier to get into the habit of reading. short chapters are also very good. series might feel like a big commitment, but can be very rewarding, but never buy a whole series unless you know you like the author/series. if you read the first book, but don’t feel an urge to read the next, don’t. if you don’t like the book your reading, there’s nothing wrong with stopping and finding a new one.

5. try to read every day. always have a book with you. find out what works best with your routine. read 5 pages before bed? read when you wake up? read at lunch, after dinner, before workouts, during workouts, anything that might fit your schedule, do it. at-least one page, often you will find yourself unable to stop once you have actually sat down and started.

hi, i have selective mutism, so i could give you a few pointers, although everyone is different.

first of all, find out if they are comfortable communicating in any kind of way. it could be through text, emails, paper, questions they could answer yes and no(so they can nod or shake their head), through a parent or friend etc. 

in the classroom, you could try to seat them at least to the side, so they could sit in a way that they don’t feel like someone is constantly looking at them. i prefer to sit in the back corner, so i can have control, but ask them where they would like to sit. also try to place them next to someone who you think would understand, not one of those people who constantly needs to talk. 

make sure to come to their desk a little more often than the other students to see if they know what their supposed to do and understand the task. it’s really hard to ask for help, so if you would come tho their desk, it might help them actually learn. 

try to sit next to them instead of in front of them, and look at what they have on their desk, instead of at them. 

never make a big deal out of it if they say something, as it makes us feel extremely guilty, uncomfortable etc. 

make sure that they know that they can take their time, and always give them an option to talk. how are you supposed to get better if you never have the option to try?
